title: SpikePingpong: Spike Vision-based Fast-Slow Pingpong Robot System
one_liner: A robot plays table tennis by splitting the problem into a fast physics-based trajectory detector and a slower learned neural refinement, then planning strikes from demonstrations.
lead: A robot has to hit a fast-moving ball at exactly the right spot and angle. Traditional approaches either rely on expensive high-speed cameras or train policies in simulation that break in the real world. SpikePingpong uses a two-stage perception system inspired by human thinking: a rapid, physics-based tracker that predicts where the ball will be, followed by a learned neural step that corrects the tracker's mistakes. For striking, it learns the right arm motions by watching human demonstrations.

problem.h2: Why fast robots miss the ball
paras: A robot playing table tennis faces two hard problems: it must watch a ball bouncing across the table at 10 meters per second, predict exactly where it will be when the paddle reaches it, and then move the arm to strike it in just milliseconds. A naive robot might use classical physics (if the ball is moving downward at this speed, it will be here in 50 milliseconds), but physics alone cannot account for spin, air resistance, or imperfections in the initial measurement. Another approach is to train a neural network end-to-end in simulation, but when the robot runs the learned policy on a real table with a real ball, the policy fails because the simulation was not accurate enough.

Existing robotic table tennis systems solve this by using very expensive high-speed cameras, or by hand-engineering the control strategy, or by relying on perfect simulation. None of these is practical: the cameras cost tens of thousands of dollars, hand-engineering requires a roboticist for each task, and simulation almost always leaves the real robot stranded.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Use a physics-based detector as the first quick step, let a learned neural network fix its mistakes as the second step, and learn striking motions directly from watching humans.

steps.text: RGB-D camera captures ball position and depth in under 1 millisecond.
System 1 uses equations of motion (accounting for initial speed, spin, air resistance) to forecast where the ball will be at time T.
System 2 collects training data showing how often System 1's prediction was wrong and learns a neural network to predict the error, then adds that correction to System 1's guess.
Given the corrected hittable position and a target zone on the opponent's side, the IMPACT module (trained on human demonstrations) selects the exact arm joint angles to send the ball to the target.
Arm moves to intercept the ball within the 50 millisecond window available from detection to impact.

paras: Instead of either trusting pure physics or trusting a learned model entirely, the paper integrates them sequentially: physics provides a fast first guess, and a learned neural network refines that guess. The two stages run in parallel hardware: System 1 (fast) runs on a fixed-function physics engine and standard camera, System 2 (slower) runs a small neural network that has time to correct before the strike must happen. This two-stage perception is combined with a third learned module (IMPACT) that chooses the striking strategy.
object.object: Prediction path: physics plus learned correction

hidden.name: How far the predicted strike location misses reality
paras: The hidden quantity is the gap between where a physics-based model predicts the ball will be and where it actually is when the paddle can hit it. This gap includes all the physics the simple model missed: spin, air drag, vibration in the table, imperfections in the initial measurement. System 1 (the fast physics engine) makes a prediction, and that prediction has an error measured in centimeters. System 2 learns to estimate this error from data.

The paper estimates this error by collecting real-world data from an automated ball launcher firing balls with varying spin and speed, recording where the physics model said the ball would land versus where it actually ended up. A neural network trained on this dataset learns to map (current ball position, current velocity, trajectory history) to the prediction error. At runtime, System 2 adds its learned error correction to System 1's physics guess, reducing the final error from ~45 centimeters (System 1 alone) to ~12 centimeters (System 1 + System 2).

heat.caption: Darker cells show large errors in System 1 alone; lighter cells show how System 2 reduces them.

reads.html: System 1 guesses. System 2 measures how much System 1 is usually wrong and learns to predict that amount of wrongness.

The Spike-Oriented Neural Improvement Calibrator (System 2) learns a Transformer-based model that predicts the deviation vector (the difference between the physics prediction and ground truth) and adds this learned deviation to the System 1 output.

mechanism.h2: Why a two-stage system works better than either alone
paras: Physics-based prediction is fast and requires no training data, but it misses real-world effects (spin creates sideways forces, air resistance is not always linear, the table vibrates). A fully learned neural network could capture these effects but requires thousands of demonstrations and takes too long to run at millisecond scale.

The paper's insight is that the two stages have different computational budgets and different knowledge. System 1 has to run in under 1 millisecond (hard deadline), so it uses a simple physics model. System 2 has 30 to 50 milliseconds until impact, so it can afford to run a neural network on the trajectory history. System 1's prediction is almost always in the right ballpark (within 50 cm), so System 2 only has to learn small corrections, which is a much easier learning problem than predicting from scratch. The combination generalizes to new conditions: if the scene has a spin rate or ball wear not seen during training, System 1 still gives a reasonable first guess, and System 2's learned correction adapts to what it observes.

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the physics model predicts the ball will be at position (50, 30, 20 cm) at impact time.
System 2 has learned that for this spin rate and table state, the physics model typically overshoots by 12 cm in the horizontal direction and undercounts vertical effect by 5 cm.
Real ball lands at (37, 34, 19 cm), so the error is now ~2 cm instead of the original 14 cm.

math.note: The final position is not learned end-to-end; instead, the paper layers fast physics on top and learns only the gap, so the system inherits physics' speed and stability while gaining accuracy from learning.

charts.title: Physics alone (System 1 only)
charts.note: System 1 (classical physics) is reliable but inaccurate; it never has catastrophic failures but misses by ~45 centimeters on average.

charts.title: Physics plus learned correction (System 1 + System 2)
charts.note: Adding the learned correction layer cuts the typical error from 45 cm to 12 cm, enough to hit 30 cm target zones reliably.

items.html: If the ball is spun in a way not seen during System 2 training, the neural correction may not adapt fast enough. Mitigation: train System 2 on a wide range of spin rates, or add online adaptation during real strikes.

If the camera or neural network introduces too much delay, the corrected prediction arrives too late and the arm misses the 50 millisecond strike window. Mitigation: keep System 1 hardware fast and System 2 network small.

items.b: Poor initial ball detection fails the whole chain.
items.html: If the camera misses the ball or gives a very noisy initial position, both System 1 and System 2 predictions start from a bad state and cannot recover. Mitigation: use a high-frame-rate camera and filter noisy measurements.

When trained on real human demonstrations and robot data, the full system (detection + System 1 + System 2 + IMPACT) hits the target zone in 47% of trials against new players with only 100 demonstrations, showing that the approach generalizes.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: A demo should show: (1) A physics-based baseline predicting ball landing position on a simple trajectory (spin-free). (2) Collect real trajectory data showing where physics is wrong. (3) Train a small neural network on the errors. (4) Run both the baseline and the corrected system on held-out trajectories and measure median absolute error (MAE) in centimeters. (5) Show that adding the neural correction cuts error by at least a factor of 2 or 3. Ideally use real video frames from a table-tennis setup; if not available, simulate trajectories with realistic air drag and spin.
demo.closing: The demo must show that the learned correction layer actually reduces typical prediction error by a significant amount—visibly and numerically.
